title: The American Heart Association Just Said Exercise Protects Your Heart Even if You Never Lose Weight. South Asians Need to Hear This.
excerpt: A landmark scientific statement in Circulation says physical activity reduces cardiovascular risk independent of the scale. For a community with the highest heart disease rates in the country, the implications are urgent.
body:
The American Heart Association has just published the clearest statement it has ever made about physical activity and obesity: exercise protects your heart even if you do not lose a single pound. For a diaspora community that leads the nation in cardiovascular risk — and is increasingly turning to weight-loss drugs like Wegovy and Ozempic — this is the most important health message of the year.

The scientific statement, titled *Role of Physical Activity in Obesity Treatment and Cardiometabolic Health*, was published in *Circulation*, the AHA's flagship peer-reviewed journal. It synthesises decades of evidence into a single directive: physical activity improves blood pressure, insulin sensitivity, cholesterol levels, and cardiorespiratory fitness in adults with overweight or obesity, independent of whether the scale moves.

## The Findings in Detail

"Doctors and health professionals often focus on weight loss to help people lower their risk of heart disease," said Dr Damon L. Swift, associate professor of kinesiology at the University of Virginia and chair of the writing group. "Physical activity delivers powerful heart and metabolic health gains even when the scale doesn't move."

The statement lays out the numbers plainly. Exercise by itself rarely produces more than a 5 per cent loss in body weight unless someone is active for 225 to 420 minutes per week — far more than most people manage. Fewer than 15 per cent of people achieve clinically significant weight loss through exercise alone.

But that is precisely the point. The AHA is saying that the benefits of exercise should not be measured by the bathroom scale. Physical activity independently reduces blood pressure, improves how the body processes insulin, raises HDL cholesterol, and strengthens the heart and lungs. These benefits occur whether someone loses weight or not.

The statement also warns about the GLP-1 era. When people lose weight through diet alone — or through medications like semaglutide — they often lose muscle along with fat. Adding exercise, particularly resistance training, helps preserve lean mass. This is critical because muscle is not merely cosmetic: it drives metabolism, stabilises blood sugar, and protects against falls and fractures as people age.

## Why the Diaspora Cannot Afford to Skip This

According to the AHA's own 2026 statistics, only one in four American adults meets the minimum recommendation of 150 minutes per week of moderate-intensity aerobic activity. Among South Asian Americans, the numbers are likely worse. Cultural norms around physical activity, long work hours in professional and small-business settings, and dietary patterns high in refined carbohydrates create a metabolic environment where heart disease strikes earlier and harder.

The MASALA study has shown that South Asian Americans have double the rate of coronary artery calcium — a marker of heart disease — compared to other ethnic groups, even after adjusting for traditional risk factors. This excess risk is driven in part by higher insulin resistance, more visceral fat, and lower cardiorespiratory fitness.

For the growing number of NRIs on GLP-1 medications, the AHA statement carries a specific warning: do not treat the drug as a substitute for exercise. "Many of the health benefits achieved from weight loss may be reversed if the weight is gained back," Dr Swift said. "Physical activity can not only help maintain weight loss, it also may protect cardiovascular health even if some weight regain occurs."

## What You Should Actually Do

The AHA recommends a minimum of 150 minutes per week of moderate-intensity aerobic exercise — brisk walking, cycling, swimming — combined with muscle-strengthening activities on at least two days per week. For weight-loss maintenance, the bar is higher: 200 to 300 minutes per week.

The statement also introduces the 5A model for clinicians: Assess, Advise, Agree, Assist, and Arrange — a structured framework for integrating exercise prescriptions into routine medical care.

For South Asian families, the message distils to a sentence: move your body, regardless of what the scale says. The heart does not care about your weight. It cares about whether you are moving.
